rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.5-2.8 and 3 - the authors run their own WEAP/AquaCrop simulations for the Chichaoua-Mejjate basin under five Med-CORDEX RCMs, two RCPs and five management scenarios, and report net precipitation, crop cycle, crop water demand, unmet demand and aquifer balance outputs (Tables 5-6, Figures 7-14).
rows.notes: The study is a scenario-modelling exercise, not an empirical test of drip irrigation. Drip appears only in Scenario 2 (Section 2.8.4), where 50% of the gravity-irrigated PMH area is switched to drip together with concreting 70% of earth canals; the reported savings (annual demand reduced ~4%, unmet demand reduced 39-41%, Douirane shortage cut 73-74%; Section 3.5, Figure 11) are a direct arithmetic consequence of assumed plot efficiencies (60% surface vs 95% drip, Table 3, taken from Le Page et al. 2020) and are confounded with the canal-lining measure. The scenario output is never compared with measured water use under drip in the real system; the only calibration mentioned is matching AquaCrop output to the Agriculture Department's conventional crop water demand figures, which is not a measurement of the drip effect. Under the rule that a model counts only when checked against observations, Q2 is 'no'. The existing private-irrigation drip perimeters (IP, 21,000 ha) are modelled with the 95% efficiency assumption but are also described as over-irrigating and driving a 2 m/year water-table decline, so the study offers no observed evidence that drip optimises water use. The paper does note that improved efficiency reduces percolation recharge to the aquifer, but this is a model consequence of the efficiency assumption, not a measured limitation.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a WEAP + AquaCrop integrated modelling framework for a Moroccan basin under RCP4.5/8.5 with five management scenarios; no field measurements of irrigation technology performance are reported.
